1.pericope_label: The plot of the chief priests and the bargain of Judas

schools.summary: Gill takes the seven days of unleavened bread as a memorial of the haste in which Israel left Egypt, having no time to leaven the dough, and as a figure of the sincerity and truth with which the gospel feast is to be kept; he adds the elders to the chief priests and scribes as making up the sanhedrim, and places their meeting not in the temple but in the palace of Caiaphas. On the bargain he has Judas undertaking the delivery and binding himself by promise, noting that the word can also mean to give thanks and that some have read it so.

Henry sees the year of the redeemed arriving in the very first month of that year, so much in haste was the Redeemer to perform his undertaking, and in the same month in which God by Moses brought Israel out of Egypt, that the antitype might answer the type. He sets the chief priests, men of sanctity, beside the scribes, men of learning, seeking to kill him by force or fraud and stopped only by their fear of the people, and observes that it is hard to say whether more mischief is done to Christ’s kingdom by the power and policy of its open enemies or by the treachery of its pretended friends.

Clarke holds that the great mass of the people were convinced that Christ was at least a prophet sent from God, and that the multitude clamouring for his blood at the crucifixion was a mere mob formed out of the creatures of the chief priests and Pharisees; on Judas he says the devil filled his heart with avarice, and turns it upon the reader, that a minister of the gospel who loves money is constantly betraying the interests of Christ. Wesley adds that Satan is never wanting to assist those whose heart is bent upon mischief, and takes the captains for Jewish officers presiding over the guards that kept watch nightly in the temple.

Robertson distinguishes the passover of Nisan the fourteenth from the unleavened bread of the fifteenth to the twenty-first, notes that the full phrase occurs only here in the New Testament, and reads the imperfect as describing the delay, since it was the manner and not the will that stalled the priests after the triumphal entry had shown Christ’s power with the crowds; he holds that Judas opened the door to Satan himself and that this in no way relieves him of moral responsibility. Barnes denies that Satan entered the body personally and makes it an influence brought to bear on a besetting passion, the tempter commonly working by raising a man’s own passions to their highest pitch. Lightfoot doubts that the Roman officers of the castle of Antonia would be called captains of the temple, since it does not appear that they had conspired against Christ; Ellicott makes them the officers set over the Levite guardians of the temple, whose sentinels carried clubs against any sacrilegious intruder.

Chrysostom makes the actions of the Jews a shadow of our own: ask a Jew what the Passover means and he will tell you nothing momentous, only the deliverance from Egypt, whereas the Christian hears not of Egypt or Pharaoh but of freedom from sin and the darkness of Satan, wrought not by Moses but by the Son of God. Theophylact marks the transition, that the evangelist having said the priests sought a way to slay him without danger now relates the way that offered itself. Titus of Bostra says Satan entered Judas not by force but finding the door open, since Judas, forgetful of all that he had seen, had turned his thoughts wholly to covetousness, and holds that the phrase one of the twelve is added because he made up the number without truly discharging the apostolic office.

Bede notes that the Passover is named not from the Passion but from the passing over, judges that the priests did not apprehend sedition but feared that by the interference of the people Christ would be taken out of their hands, and reconciles John’s notice that Satan entered Judas after the sop by distinguishing an entry as a stranger from an entry as his own. Tertullian presses the choice of this feast against those who would part Christ from the law: he knew the time it behoved him to suffer because the law prefigured his passion, and of all the festal days he chose the one in which Moses had declared a sacred mystery; he might have been betrayed by a stranger and without a price, but a psalm had said that he who ate bread with him would lift up his heel, and Jeremiah had named both the price and the potter’s field.

debates: In what sense Satan entered into Judas: Barnes denies any personal entry into the body and makes it an influence on an existing passion, Titus of Bostra says the tempter found the door already open, Bede distinguishes this entry as a stranger from the later entry after the sop as his own, and Robertson insists that whichever it was, the moral responsibility stays with Judas

Who the captains were: Lightfoot doubts that the Roman officers of Antonia would be so called and looks instead to the temple watches, while Ellicott and Wesley take them for the officers set over the Levite guard
outliers: Tertullian asks whether Christ longed to keep the passover because he was so fond of Jewish lamb, and answers that it was because he had to be led like a lamb to the slaughter
Chrysostom contrasts what a Jew and a Christian will each tell you the Passover means, the one naming Egypt and the other freedom from sin
Clarke turns the avarice of Judas directly on the ministry, that a preacher who loves money betrays the interests of Christ continually

7.pericope_label: The preparing of the Passover: the two disciples, the man with the pitcher, and the upper room

schools.summary: Gill fixes the day as the first of the days of unleavened bread, the fourteenth of Nisan, notes that Jesus and not the disciples did the sending, and observes that the question where the disciples should prepare was never about which town, since it was a settled thing that the passover could be eaten only at Jerusalem, but only about which house within it; the man bearing the pitcher he takes for a servant and the goodman of the house for his master.

Henry holds that Christ was made under the law and kept its ordinances, the passover in particular, to teach us in like manner not to neglect his own gospel institutions; that he could easily have described a house the disciples probably knew, and directed them by a sign instead to teach them to follow the conduct of Providence step by step, going without knowing whither they went or whom they followed, so that they need not fear disappointment who go upon Christ’s word. He notes too that Judas was admitted to sit down with the rest, since those whose hearts are filled with Satan may still keep up a plausible profession while the wickedness does not break out into open scandal.

Clarke distinguishes the two uses of the word, the name of the festival itself from the name of that on which they feasted, namely the sacrificed paschal lamb, and refers the reader to his fuller treatment of the preparation in the parallel chapter of Matthew.

Robertson notes that the day itself came rather than merely drew nigh, that the lamb was to be slain by the head of the family, and that Luke, writing as a Gentile, presents as plain fact the reckoning the Synoptics share, which the five passages in John rightly interpreted do not contradict; he observes the deliberative subjunctive in the disciples’ question and the late Greek compound for the goodman of the house. Ellicott points out that Luke alone gives the names of the two sent, that they appear together repeatedly afterwards, and that a loving insight may be recognised in the act which brought them together at a time when our Lord foresaw how much one would need the love and sympathy of the other; the signal of the man with the pitcher he treats as a detail common to Mark and Luke.

Titus of Bostra states the logic of the day in a sentence, that in order to leave us a heavenly Passover our Lord ate a typical one, removing the figure that the truth might take its place. Theophylact names the two sent as the loving and the loved, says that in all things to the very end of his life Christ opposed not the law, and explains that he was sent to a strange house because he and his disciples had none of their own; the anonymity of the householder he takes as proof that Christ underwent the Passion willingly, since one who could so sway a stranger’s mind could have dealt with the Jews as he wished, though he reports the other opinion that the name was withheld lest the traitor learn it. The water he reads as the grace of the Holy Spirit and the pitcher as humbleness of heart, since grace is given to the humble who know themselves earth and dust.

Cyril of Alexandria makes the whole design voluntary: though his right hand is almighty and his power overthrows both corruption and death, he submitted of his own accord, by becoming flesh, to the tasting of death for the life of all, and the rebellious serpent, imagining that he had prevailed because Christ suffered death in the flesh, was disappointed of his expectation. Origen keeps the man with the pitcher a real servant carrying water for washing or drinking, then reads him as Moses conveying spiritual doctrine in fleshly histories, and warns that those who do not follow him, and those taken up with banquetings and worldly cares, neither ascend into the upper part of the house nor keep the Passover with Jesus.

Bede fixes the date as the fourteenth day of the first month, when the leaven having been put away the lamb was held toward evening, and hears the disciples’ question as a confession that they have no abode and no place of shelter, bidding those who busy themselves in building houses know that Christ, the Lord of all places, had nowhere to lay his head; the house to which the water is carried he makes the place where the typical blood is taken from the lintel and the baptism of the life-giving fountain is consecrated to take away sin. Ambrose bids us observe first the greatness of the divine power, that while talking with his disciples Christ knows what will happen in another place, and next the condescension by which he seeks out not the rich or powerful but the poor, preferring a mean inn to the spacious palaces of nobles, the man being left unnamed that he may be counted as ignoble; the pitcher he calls a more perfect measure and the water that which was thought meet to be a sacrament of Christ, to wash and not to be washed.

debates: Why the householder is left unnamed: Ambrose says it is that he may be counted as ignoble, Theophylact makes the anonymity a proof that the Passion was undergone willingly while reporting the alternative that the name was hidden from the traitor

How far the sign is to be read allegorically: Origen keeps the water-carrier a real servant before turning him into Moses, Theophylact makes the water the Spirit and the pitcher humility, Ambrose makes it a measure and Bede makes the house the place of baptism, while Ellicott and Robertson treat the whole as narrative detail shared with Mark
outliers: Bede turns the disciples’ question into a rebuke of those who busy themselves in building houses, since Christ the Lord of all places had nowhere to lay his head
Origen shuts the banqueters and the worldly out of the upper room, holding that they do not keep the Passover with Jesus at all
The Cyril of Alexandria material filed at this point is his exposition of the preceding passage, the plot and the bargain of Judas, and stands one section later than the text it comments on

14.pericope_label: The paschal meal begun: the desire to eat it, the first cup, and the Passover fulfilled

schools.summary: Gill puts the hour after six o’clock, at the last of the two evenings, notes that the passover with the rest of the ceremonial law was now to be abolished, and counts the four cups of wine which the poorest man in Israel was obliged to drink at the passover, each with a blessing pronounced over it, taking the cup here for the first of them. Calvin asks whether the two cups of this account are one thing told twice or two separate acts, and judges them two, since the holy fathers observed a solemn rite of tasting the cup during sacrifices, whence the Psalmist speaks of taking the cup of salvation and calling on the name of the Lord; Christ kept that ancient custom before turning to a new mystery which was a wholly different institution from the paschal lamb, and gave thanks then as he never sat down at table without calling on God.

Clarke reads the doubled verb as a Hebraism for the most earnest desire, and makes it the longing of one who, having purposed to redeem a lost world by his blood, ardently desired the hour of offering himself up; the fulfilment he refers to the death through which the kingdom of God was to be established among men. On the cup he agrees that this was not the sacramental cup, which came after supper, and pictures it handed from the first person on Christ’s right hand round to the last on his left. Wesley divides the desire between the disciples, to whom Christ would manifest himself further at this solemn parting, and the whole Church, for which he would institute the grand memorial of his death, and puts the proper commencement of the kingdom at the resurrection.

Ellicott calls the cognate noun with its verb a characteristically Hebrew idiom and infers that Luke heard the saying from someone who repeated the very words spoken in Aramaic, the whole passage being peculiar to him and implying that he sought to fill the gaps in the oral teaching the other Gospels reproduce; the fulfilment he finds both in the sacrifice on the cross and in every commemoration of it, each such act being a communion of the disciples with one another and with Christ, and in the first cup he sees, from the uncommon word for dividing, an anticipation of the tongues parted at Pentecost and so of the several gifts of the one Spirit. Barnes supposes that Christ, about to leave them, wished once to see them together and to share one of the religious privileges of the Jewish dispensation, never having undervalued the rites of his country, and holds that this cup was not the sacramental one but a passover cup on which the new ordinance was ingrafted. Robertson notes that the verb of sitting down means reclining, that the doubled desire is a Septuagint Hebraism, that the verb of thanksgiving here is the one from which Eucharist comes, and that the fulfilment seems to look to a Messianic banquet.

Theophylact meets the objection that the Jews ate the Passover standing by answering that when the legal Passover had been eaten they sat down by common custom to the rest of their food; he hears in the doubled desire the tone of a farewell, as those going away to a distance utter their last words most affectionately, and takes the kingdom for the resurrection, which is so called because it has destroyed death, adding that Christ drinks again with his disciples afterwards to prove the resurrection no shadow. Chrysostom says simply that after this Passover the Cross was at hand, and draws from the thanksgiving a rule for the table, that hunger should be satisfied with moderation because after the meal one must pray, and that food should be followed not by sleep or rest but by prayer and the reading of Scripture.

Cyril of Alexandria explains the secrecy that made the meal possible, that the covetous disciple was watching for a time to betray his Master, and that in order that he might not betray him before the feast our Lord had divulged neither the house nor the man with whom he would keep the Passover; the words themselves, he says, make this plain enough.

Bede dates the hour to the fourteenth day of the first month far gone toward evening, with the fifteenth moon just appearing on the earth, and has Christ approving the legal Passover and then, having taught that it was the figure of his own dispensation, forbidding it henceforth to be represented in the flesh: he will celebrate the Mosaic Passover no more until, spiritually understood, it is fulfilled in the Church, which is the kingdom of God. The thanksgiving over the cup he explains as given because the old things were about to pass away and all things to become new.

debates: Whether this cup belongs to the institution: Barnes, Clarke, Gill and Ellicott agree that it is one of the passover cups and that the sacramental cup came after supper, while Calvin argues that the two cups are two distinct acts, Christ first tasting by the ancient rite and only then turning to the new mystery

In what kingdom the Passover is fulfilled: Bede makes it the Church, Wesley and Theophylact the resurrection, Clarke the kingdom established by Christ’s death, Ellicott both the cross and every commemoration of it, and Robertson a Messianic banquet still to come
outliers: Chrysostom turns the thanksgiving into a rule about meals, that one should eat with moderation because prayer follows, and that food should be succeeded by prayer and Scripture rather than sleep
Ellicott connects the rare word for dividing this cup with the tongues parted at Pentecost, and so reads the first cup as a symbol of the distributed gifts of the Spirit

19.pericope_label: The institution of the Lord’s Supper: the bread broken, the cup after supper, and the new covenant

schools.summary: Gill observes that the account of the Lord’s supper begins only at this point, the passover having been eaten first, and that the cup was taken after they had eaten the bread, thanks being given over it before it was handed to the disciples. Calvin fastens on the clause which the other evangelists omit and which is far from superfluous, since the reason the flesh of Christ becomes life-giving to us is that by it salvation was once procured; whoever desires that flesh to nourish him must look at it as having been offered on the cross to be the price of our reconciliation with God, and the same observation must be extended to the cup.

Henry makes the supper a sign and memorial of a Christ already come, who by dying delivered us, his death being in a special manner set before us in the ordinance: the breaking of his body as a sacrifice is brought to remembrance by the breaking of bread and the shedding of his blood by the wine in the cup. Nothing, he holds, can be more nourishing and satisfying to the soul than the doctrine of Christ making atonement for sin and the assurance of an interest in that atonement, so that the act is at once a remembrance of what he did for us and a memorial of what we do in joining ourselves to him in an everlasting covenant.

Clarke reports from the rabbins that the Jews in eating the passover meant to represent the sufferings of the Messiah, the great hallel sung after the paschal supper comprehending the exodus from Egypt, the dividing of the Red Sea, the promulgation of the law, the resurrection of the dead and those sufferings; he paraphrases the cup as signifying the blood of the new covenant shortly to be ratified by the shedding of his own, and remarks that Christ handed neither bread nor cup to each person but gave it to the man next him to be passed along, so that the present mode of administering the supper is not strictly according to the original institution. Wesley places the bread some time after, when the paschal supper was ended, argues that since Christ had just kept the supper called the passover he uses like figurative language of the bread, and that this alone was enough to prevent anyone supposing it his real body any more than the lamb was really the passover; the cup he calls an undeniable figure standing for the wine in it, and the New Testament in his blood not the covenant itself but its seal and sign.

Lightfoot finds the formula built on antithesis and allusion, since the Jews used the very phrase the body of the Passover of the paschal lamb, so that the sense is that by the same signification by which the lamb was my body hitherto, from henceforth let this bread be my body; he notes too that the apostle adds broken for you where the Gospel has given. Robertson reports that some manuscripts omit these verses, thinks them genuine, observes that the true text elsewhere reads which is for you rather than which is broken for you though the longer reading is still often defended, takes the command as a present imperative of repetition, and sets out the textual difficulty of the two cups, since without the longer reading Luke would have the cup before the bread. Ellicott prefers the rendering new covenant, notes that both the adjective and the shed for you are peculiar to Luke in the best manuscripts, that the participle is present, being shed, like the being given before it, and that Paul and Luke agree in placing the cup after they had supped.

Theophylact counts the two cups of this account, the first a type of the Old Testament and the second imparted by Christ himself after the breaking and giving of the bread, and hears the Lord calling this second one the New Testament in his blood. Chrysostom presses what the blood entails upon the communicant: it moulds a royal image in us, suffers not the nobleness of the soul to waste away, puts the devils to flight and summons angels and the Lord of angels, and being poured forth washed the world and made heaven open; yet if a man come polluted by an evil conscience he comes to his own destruction, for if those who defile the imperial purple are punished like those who tear it asunder, it is not unreasonable that they who receive Christ with an unclean heart should be beaten with the stripes of those who pierced him with nails. Cyril of Jerusalem sets the table of the psalm against another table: before Christ’s coming the evil spirits had prepared one polluted and full of devilish influence, and God has now spread this mystical and spiritual table over against it, the one having communion with devils and the other with God.
Gregory of Nyssa states the change without argument: the bread before the consecration is common bread, but when the mystery has consecrated it, it is, and it is called, the Body of Christ.

Bede marks the hinge of the chapter, that the rites of the old Passover being finished Christ passes to the new, which he would have the Church celebrate in memory of his redemption, putting in place of the flesh and blood of the lamb the sacrament of his own under the figure of bread and wine, being made a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek. The thanksgiving here answers the thanksgiving at the close of the old feast and leaves us an example to glorify God at the beginning and the end of every good work; and Christ breaks with his own hands the bread he holds out, to show that the breaking of his body, that is his Passion, will not be against his will.

debates: In what sense the bread is the body: Lightfoot and Wesley argue from the Jewish phrase for the paschal lamb that the language is figurative in exactly the way the passover was, while Gregory of Nyssa holds that after consecration the bread is and is called the Body, and Chrysostom reasons from a real reception of Christ to the danger of receiving unworthily

How the two cups are to be ordered: Theophylact makes the first a type of the Old Testament and the second the New, while Robertson lays out the textual problem, that the documents which omit the longer reading leave Luke with the cup standing before the bread
outliers: Clarke reports the rabbinic answer to why the hallel is called great, namely that it contains the exodus, the dividing of the sea, the giving of the law, the resurrection of the dead and the sufferings of the Messiah
Clarke observes that Christ handed the elements to the man beside him to be passed along, and concludes that the present mode of administering the supper departs from the original institution

21.pericope_label: The hand of the betrayer on the table, and the woe pronounced upon him

schools.summary: Gill takes the hand literally, of the hand of Judas then dipping in the dish with Christ rather than of his counsel and conspiracy, and glosses the going of the Son of man simply as dying, which is going the way of all the earth. He notes that two days earlier at Bethany the same hint had left the disciples looking at one another, unable for a while to speak either to Christ or to each other, whereas now they inquire both among themselves and of Christ.

Henry argues from the order of the narrative that Judas received the sacrament, since Luke places these words after the institution where Matthew and Mark place them before, so that Judas did eat of that bread and drink of that cup, and there have been those who ate bread with Christ and yet betrayed him. He holds that Christ was not driven to his sufferings but went cheerfully to them, and that neither the patience of the saints under their sufferings nor the counsel of God concerning them will be any excuse for those who have a hand in them, Judas’s sin and punishment being not at all the less for God having determined the betrayal. He notes too that the disciples’ question was not whether it was another but whether it was oneself.

Clarke reproduces Lightfoot’s argument as his own, that nothing could be desired more as a demonstration that Judas was present at the eucharist, and that the contrary case from the thirteenth chapter of John is made out of nothing since there is not a syllable there of the paschal supper but only of a supper before the feast; he observes besides that the best Greek and Latin writers use the words for going away in the sense of dying. Wesley denies the conclusion flatly, holding that Christ spoke these words before the institution, since the other evangelists put the sop immediately before Judas went out, and the sop could not have been dipped or given except while the meat was still on the table, which was all removed before the bread and the cup were brought.

Lightfoot asks what more could be desired as a demonstration that Judas was present at the eucharist, and dismisses the contrary argument from John as making something out of nothing. Robertson records the difference of order without deciding it, that Luke narrates the institution before the exposure of the traitor while Mark and Matthew reverse it, notes that the participle has Judas actually engaged in the act with his hand resting on the table at that moment, and observes that the perfect participle of the determining marks off a border like a horizon, yet does not absolve Judas of the guilt the woe makes plain. Ellicott finds the word rendered determined eminently characteristic of Luke, and holds that the woe, standing in all three of the first Gospels, must be reckoned among the sayings that made an indelible impression on the hearers, reproduced word for word amid many variations elsewhere.

Theophylact says the announcement was made not only to show that Christ knew all things but to declare his own especial goodness, since he left nothing undone that belonged to him to do, and gives us an example that even to the end we should be employed in reclaiming sinners; it exposes besides the baseness of a traitor who blushed not to be his guest, and the going of the Son of man is not that of one unable to preserve himself but of one determining for himself to suffer death for the salvation of man. Chrysostom presses it harder: though Judas partook of the mystery he was not converted, and his wickedness is made only the more awful both because he came to it under the pollution of such a design and because in coming he was made no better by fear, gratitude or respect; the woe is added lest anyone should deem him guiltless as the minister of a dispensation.

Basil, cited on the disciples asking after a sin of which they had no consciousness, compares the diseases of the body, many of which the sufferer does not feel, so that he puts more faith in the opinion of his physician than in his own insensibility; so also in the diseases of the soul a man who is conscious of no sin in himself ought still to trust those able to know more of it than he does.

Bede notes that our Lord does not point the traitor out by name, lest being plainly detected he grow the more shameless, but throws the charge upon the whole twelve so that the guilty one might be turned to repentance, and proclaims the punishment so that one whom shame had not moved might be brought to amendment by the sentence denounced; he adds that the woe falls also on the man who comes unworthily to the Lord’s table and after the example of Judas betrays the Son, not to Jews but to sinners, that is to his own sinful members. Augustine sets the saying in its place, that when our Lord had given the cup he spoke again of his betrayer. Tertullian turns the woe into an argument: it must be the imprecation of an angry Master unless Judas was to escape with impunity after so vast a sin, and if Christ knowingly permitted a man he had deliberately chosen for a companion to plunge into so great a crime, then the argument brought against the Creator in Adam’s case recoils upon those who bring it, who must charge their own God either with ignorance, or with inability, or with unwillingness to hinder the sinner he foresaw.

debates: Whether Judas received the Lord’s Supper: Lightfoot, Clarke and Henry all conclude that he did, the first two from the silence of John about the paschal supper and the third from Luke’s placing the exposure after the institution, while Wesley denies it on the ground that the sop belongs to a table already cleared before the bread and cup were brought, and Robertson records the difference of order without deciding

How the determinate counsel bears on the traitor’s guilt: Henry and Robertson insist that the determining leaves the guilt untouched, Chrysostom adds the woe expressly lest anyone think Judas guiltless as a minister of the dispensation, and Tertullian argues from the woe that a foreknowing God who permits a chosen companion to sin cannot be charged on that account with the fault
outliers: Bede reads the woe as falling also on unworthy communicants, who betray the Son not to Jews but to their own sinful members
Basil justifies the disciples’ question about a sin they were not conscious of by the analogy of bodily diseases the patient cannot feel

24.pericope_label: The strife over greatness, the rule of service, and the kingdom appointed to the apostles

schools.summary: Gill reports the suspicion that this contention belongs to the earlier occasion when the mother of Zebedee’s sons asked for the two chief places, and that Luke has inserted it out of its proper place, while noting that the Ethiopic version pins it to this very time and that what gave occasion to it may have been what Christ had just said about the kingdom. The kingdom appointed he takes as spiritual and not temporal, the government of the church committed to the apostles as those set in the first place and office in it, with the keys of the Gospel dispensation and the power of binding and loosing; the eating and drinking at Christ’s table he refers to the Gospel church state, to the marriage supper of the Lamb and to the ultimate glory. Calvin holds that Luke here relates detached sentences without regard to the order of time and yet refers them to this occasion, takes the temptations for the contests by which God tried the Master and the apostles in common, since by the feeling of human nature Christ’s own faith and patience were actually tried, and weighs the verb of appointing as a check upon those who would hasten too eagerly to possess what he alone has the right to dispose; the example is a call to patience, for though ordained a King he was not at once raised to his glory but obtained kingly honour by the ignominy of the cross.

Clarke separates two earlier contentions and identifies this one with the dispute occasioned by the request of Zebedee’s wife, so that Luke has recorded it much out of the order of time; he notes that the Greek for benefactor was the actual surname of some of the Ptolemies, and that Rome distributed conquered frontier lands to her soldiers, who were thence called beneficiaries, so that it is no wonder sovereigns however oppressive were called benefactors by men dependent on their bounty. Following Lightfoot he places the strife between Peter and the sons of Zebedee, the younger disciples taking no part, and he records both the variant which puts covenant for kingdom in the first clause and the fact that Marcion left the verse about the thrones out altogether, probably because he did not understand it. Wesley agrees that this is the dispute Matthew and Mark relate and therefore happened earlier, says shortest of all that they who exercise the most arbitrary authority have from their flatterers the vain title of benefactors, and insists that what is appointed is not a primacy to one but a kingdom to every one on the same terms.

Barnes finds nothing more humiliating than that, just as Jesus was contemplating his own death and labouring to prepare them for it, the disciples should contend about office and rank; he denies that Christ condemns the authority of kings as such, holding only that his kingdom is of another character, and observes that the title of benefactor was applied to kings by way of compliment or flattery and especially to the Roman emperors. Ellicott holds the incident peculiar to Luke, its noun for strife occurring nowhere else in the New Testament, asks whether the candidates were Peter with the keys, John on the Master’s bosom or Andrew the first called, finds the emphasis falling on are called as against the let him become that follows, hears the words about the younger and the chief and the servant as already half technical in an ecclesiastical sense, and argues that the temptations cannot be the Temptation, encountered in absolute solitude, but must be the trials of the ministry. He notes too that the verb of appointing is the one from which the word covenant is formed. Lightfoot presses that the younger is properly a term of age and asks who will deny that Peter was the oldest of the company, which would explain his standing first in the catalogue, his seat next the Lord and the frequency with which Christ addressed him. Robertson glosses the rare noun as an eagerness to contend, calls the scene the tragedy of the situation with the Cross before Christ and the traitor at the table, and states the rule flatly, that true greatness is in service and not in rank.

Theophylact traces the quarrel to the question just asked, since while they inquired which of them should betray him they would naturally pass to saying you are the traitor, and thence to saying I am the greatest; he also marks the turn by which, woe having been denounced on the traitor, blessing is promised to the rest, and takes the twelve tribes to be judged as the unbelievers condemned out of them.

Cyril of Alexandria explains that by means of the things of our present life spiritual things are described, since those who sit at an earthly king’s table as guests exercise a high privilege, so that by man’s own estimation Christ shows who shall be rewarded by him with the greatest honours.

Ambrose warns that not every kind of respect and deference betokens humility, since a man may defer for the world’s sake, from fear of another’s power or regard to his own interest, and in that case seeks to edify himself rather than to honour another; the precept given to all is that they boast not about precedence but strive earnestly for humility. He adds that the reward promised is not food and drink but the communication of heavenly grace and life, since it is not equality with God but likeness to him that man must aspire to. Bede holds that the great need no little judgment under this rule, neither tyrannising over their subjects like the kings of the Gentiles nor puffed up with their praises, and yet provoked with a righteous zeal against the wickedness of offenders; and that it is not the first effort of patience but long-continued perseverance which is rewarded with the glory of the heavenly kingdom, perseverance being the pillar and prop of all the virtues.

debates: Whether this contention stands in its own place: Clarke and Wesley identify it with the earlier dispute over the sons of Zebedee and hold that Luke has related it out of the order of time, Gill reports that suspicion while noting a version which pins it here, and Calvin treats the passage as detached sentences yet refers them to this occasion, while Ellicott takes the incident as peculiar to Luke and prompted by what had just passed

What the temptations were in which the apostles continued: Ellicott and Robertson make them the trials of the ministry rather than the Temptation, which was encountered in solitude, Calvin the contests by which God tried Master and apostles together, and Wesley the whole of Christ’s life from his entering on his public ministry
outliers: Clarke explains the flattery of the title benefactor from the Roman practice of granting frontier lands to soldiers, who were called beneficiaries and were dependent on the sovereign’s bounty
Lightfoot builds a case that Peter was simply the oldest of the twelve, and explains his precedence in the lists and at table by age rather than office
Clarke records that Marcion cut out the verse about the twelve thrones altogether, probably because he did not understand it

31.pericope_label: Satan’s desire to sift the disciples, the prayer for Peter’s faith, and the denial foretold

schools.summary: Gill notes that Christ addresses Peter not by the name he had given him, which signified his future solidity and steadfastness, since in this instance he would give no proof of it, but by his former name, and doubles it to show both the earnestness of the warning and his affectionate concern; the prayer he takes to be either the one recorded in John, which touches the preservation and final perseverance of the apostles, or another and merely mental. Calvin finds Luke’s account fuller than the other two, since Christ does not simply foretell the coming trouble but expressly declares that the disciples will have a contest with Satan and at the same time promises them the victory; and he draws the admonition that whenever anything gives us offence we should have the snares of Satan before our eyes, since we wrestle not with flesh and blood but with spiritual armies.

Clarke holds that a name repeated in the sacred writings is always love speaking in a warning voice, and insists from the plural pronoun that the words were addressed not to Peter alone but to all the apostles and particularly the three contenders, Satan having already got Judas, nearly got Peter, and wishing to have all; the devil, he adds, cannot tempt a man at all unless he receive permission, and desires to do all evil while permitted only to do some. On the prayer he presses that Peter’s faith did fail but not utterly, and that he fell without falling off or apostatising as Judas did, the common rendering making the prayer look as though it had not been heard. He reconciles this day with this night by the Jewish reckoning from evening to evening. Wesley glosses the sifting as a trying to the uttermost, and reads the charge to strengthen the brethren as directed to all that are weak in faith and perhaps scandalised at Peter’s fall, noting that the usual hour of cock-crowing probably came only after the bird Peter heard had already crowed.

Ellicott hears in the doubled name the emphasis of sadness, finds both verbs in a tense which treats the act as wholly past, as though the Lord had stood in some scene like the opening of Job or the vision of Zechariah and had prevailed by his intercession, and takes the individualising pronouns to mark out the disciple most confident of his greatness as the one in most danger; faith did fail in one sense at the denial, yet repentance followed and a new power to strengthen others was gained through that weakness. Barnes explains the figure of grain shaken in a fan while the chaff is thrown off, compares the giving of Job into Satan’s hands, takes faith here for religion or attachment to Christ and the failing for total apostasy, and reasons that since God always heard his Son the specific request was granted, so that there was no moment when Peter was not really a pious man. Lightfoot turns the verse against the use made of it, asking who would have drawn an argument for the primacy of Thomas or Philip had the name been theirs, and finding here a severe chiding rather than a promotion; he observes too that the courage of the other apostles failed while their faith was never so near shipwreck as Peter’s, and that it was not much to his honour that he beyond all others needed such a prayer. Robertson glosses the first verb as begging something for oneself and the second from the winnowing fan, each found only here in the New Testament, and concludes that Jesus could not keep Satan from attacking Peter but could and did pray for his faith, the participle of turning again implying the fall.

Chrysostom observes that Christ says not I have granted but I have prayed, speaking humbly as one approaching his Passion and manifesting his human nature, since he who said with authority that upon this rock he would build his Church and would give the keys of the kingdom needed no prayer to steady one agitated soul; nor does he say I have prayed that you deny not, but that you do not abandon your faith. Theophylact says the warning came to Peter because he was bolder than the rest and might grow proud of what had been promised him, adds that though the spirit shed its leaves in temptation the root held firm, and draws the doctrine that human resolve is not sufficient without divine support, since Peter for all his zeal was overthrown by the enemy when forsaken of God.

Basil holds that God sometimes allows the rash to receive a fall as a remedy for their former self-confidence, and distinguishes the rash man, who sins by reason of secret assaults and almost against his will, from those who have no care either for themselves or for God and know no difference between sin and virtue; the first needs reproof in the very thing wherein he sinned, the others must be afflicted and rebuked until they acknowledge that God is a just Judge. Cyril of Alexandria sounds the summons to awake and watch, since the enemy makes us his prey in various ways by seizing hold of our many passions and so leading us on to a reprobate mind, while those who would not be subject to his power gain the victory by the help of Christ, who cares for our souls.

Bede reads the warning as a check upon the praise just given, that lest the eleven should impute to their own strength their having almost alone among so many thousands continued with their Lord, he shows them that without his aid the same storm would have beaten them down as it beat the rest; the sifting is a longing to tempt and shake them as one who cleanses wheat by winnowing, and the whole teaches that no man’s faith is tried unless God permits it. Ambrose finds Peter earnest in spirit but weak in bodily inclination and therefore declared about to deny his Lord, since he could not equal the constancy of the divine will, our Lord’s Passion having rivals but no equal. Augustine, comparing the four accounts, notes that Matthew and Mark place the warning after the company had left the house where the Passover was eaten while Luke and John place it before, and that since not only the words but the sentences themselves differ, we are rather compelled to believe that Peter uttered his boast three times at different points of the discourse and was three times answered.

debates: Whether the prayer for Peter marks him out for honour: Theophylact and Ellicott take the singling out as a measure of his danger and his over-confidence, Barnes finds in it a provision of comfort for the hour of repentance, while Lightfoot reads it as a severe chiding and denies outright that any primacy can be built on it

In what sense Peter’s faith failed: Clarke and Barnes insist that it failed without failing utterly, so that the prayer was answered and Peter never wholly apostatised, Ellicott allows that in one sense it did fail at the denial though repentance and a new strength followed, and Robertson concludes that Christ could not prevent the attack but could and did pray, the words about turning again already implying the fall
outliers: Lightfoot tests the argument for Peter’s primacy by putting Thomas or Philip in his place, and asks who would then have found a primacy in the words
Basil turns the fall into a remedy, holding that God sometimes lets the rash fall as a cure for the self-confidence that went before

35.pericope_label: Purse, scrip and sword: the changed conditions of the mission and the two swords

schools.summary: Gill has the disciples taking the words literally, the two swords being such as they might have brought with them from Galilee to defend themselves against the thieves and robbers that infested the roads to Jerusalem, one of them Peter’s, and mentions them with a desire to know whether these were sufficient or whether more must be provided. Calvin holds that Christ had until now kept the disciples in the shade and at a distance from the enemy’s darts, treating them gently like children, so that having gathered courage and strength in that leisure they might now be employed in labour like men; the arming he makes metaphorical, a general calling soldiers to the field and bidding them lay aside every other care, so that everything must be sold to buy weapons, yet the conflict is not outward but the severe struggle of temptations to be sustained in spiritual contests. He makes the adverb of the prophecy emphatic, since Christ had not discharged every part of his office until he was ranked with the wicked as if of their class, and rejects the inference of the canonists that the two swords establish a double jurisdiction for their mitred bishops as not merely an offensive allegory but a detestable one; the disciples themselves he calls shamefully stupid for imagining, after so much teaching about the cross, that they must fight with weapons of iron.

Clarke reports Bishop Pearce’s suspicion that the word sword was inserted here from the later verse, since the verb of buying may govern the scrip instead, and holds that our Lord never intended any resistance or the use of a sword on the occasion; he reproduces Lightfoot’s gloss on the closing clause and adds that the prophecy, whatever it referred to in the prophet’s own time, could have no complete accomplishment but in the crucifixion of Christ as a criminal. At the two swords he takes the disciples’ words not as an answer to a command they had failed to keep, since two would not arm twelve, but as a declaration of readiness, Peter and perhaps others meaning that they would fight for their Master. Wesley says shortly that it is plain the words are not to be taken literally and mean only that this will be a time of extreme danger, notes that many of Galilee carried swords when they travelled because of robbers and assassins, and asks whether the apostles needed any such defence.

Barnes explains the change of conditions, that before they were sent for a little time in their own country while now they were to go into the wide world among strangers and dangers, and distinguishes carefully in the prophecy that Christ was reckoned not as a transgressor but among them, put to death in their company and treated as such though holy and undefiled; he notes too that the Galileans and the Essenes commonly went armed because the country was full of robbers and wild beasts. Ellicott finds in the appeal to the first mission a pleasant evidence that the disciples were then welcomed and received food and shelter that met all their wants, observes that had the saying stopped short of the sword it could have been taken literally without difficulty as counselling the prudence which provides for want, hears grave irony in the answer since two swords were enough and more than enough for one who did not mean them used at all, and rejects the mystical reading which finds in them the spiritual and temporal authority of Peter and his successors. He also finds the citation of the prophecy remarkable as showing that the picture of the righteous sufferer had been present all along to our Lord’s thoughts. Robertson allows that the sword is for defence but denies that the disciples are to repel force with force, observes that changed conditions bring changed needs and that the language could be misunderstood then as it is now, and notes that before the night is out Peter will use one of these very swords and be sternly rebuked, so that Christ plainly did not mean the words pressed too literally; the answer he takes for sad irony. Lightfoot asks whether the counsel is given in earnest and answers that it is common speech, the rabbins using the like of selling one’s garments to buy oil and candles for the feast of Dedication, and that Christ is warning them of a danger close at hand so as to give them such an apprehension of their enemies’ rage as would suppress their private animosities; the closing clause he glosses as meaning that Christ’s business is done and theirs only beginning.

Chrysostom illustrates the change of discipline by a swimming master, who at first holds his pupils up with his own hands and afterwards frequently withdraws them, bidding them help themselves and even letting them sink a little. On the sword he asks what this can be, that he who said if any one strike you on the right cheek turn to him the other should now arm his disciples, and with a sword only, when a man completely armed would need shield and helmet too, and when a thousand such weapons would not fit eleven men to face the attacks and ambushes of peoples, tyrants, allies and nations.

Cyril of Alexandria sets the saying immediately after the warning to Peter, since having once spoken of his being taken captive Christ goes on to announce the struggle that would ensue against the Jews; the Saviour had sent the holy apostles to preach the kingdom of heaven in the cities and towns, bidding them take no thought for the things of the body but place their whole hope of salvation in him.

Bede states the rule plainly, that Christ does not train his disciples by the same discipline in time of persecution as in time of peace: when he sent them out to preach he ordered them to take nothing on the way, ordaining that he who preaches the gospel should live by the gospel, but when the crisis of death was at hand and the whole nation persecuted both the shepherd and the flock he proposed a law adapted to the time, allowing them to take the necessaries of life until the rage of the persecutors was abated and the time of preaching had returned; and he leaves us thereby an example that when a just reason urges we may without blame intermit something of the strictness of our determination. Augustine adds that this is no inconsistency in him who commands but the reason of a dispensation. Ambrose asks why he who forbids to strike should order them to buy a sword, and answers that there may be a defence prepared but no necessary retaliation, a seeming ability to be revenged without the will.

debates: Whether the command to buy a sword is meant literally: Ambrose allows a defence prepared without the will to retaliate, Chrysostom argues from the absurdity of arming eleven men against nations that it cannot be literal, Calvin and Wesley make it wholly figurative of a time of danger, Clarke reports the conjecture that the word was inserted from the following verse, and Robertson allows a real defensive sense while denying that force may be repelled by force

What the two swords amount to: Gill and Barnes take the disciples to be answering in earnest, since Galileans travelled armed against robbers, Clarke reads the words as a declaration of readiness to fight for Christ, while Ellicott and Robertson hear grave irony in the reply, and Ellicott and Calvin both reject outright the reading which makes the two swords the spiritual and temporal authority of Peter’s successors
outliers: Chrysostom compares the change in Christ’s discipline to a swimming master who withdraws his supporting hands and lets his pupils sink a little
Bede draws from the changed rule a general licence to relax the strictness of a resolution when a just reason urges it

39.pericope_label: Gethsemane: the wonted place, the charge to pray, the kneeling and the cup

schools.summary: Gill has Christ leaving the guest-chamber and the city together, to begin his sorrows and sufferings without the camp where he was also to end them, and places the garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives; he notes that the three disciples were taken further in while the rest were left at a distance, and supplies the condition of the prayer as a consistency with the will of saving sinners which the Father had declared and the Son undertaken to perform, where the other evangelists put it as a question of possibility.

Henry sets the whole agony under that part of Christ’s undertaking which he was now entering upon, the making of his soul an offering for sin: he afflicted his own soul with grief for the sin he was to satisfy for and with an apprehension of the wrath of God to which man had by sin made himself obnoxious, which he was pleased as a sacrifice to admit the impressions of, the consuming of a sacrifice with fire from heaven being the surest token of its acceptance. In it, he says, Christ entered the lists with the powers of darkness, gave them all the advantages they could desire, and yet conquered them.
Clarke identifies the place as Gethsemane and refers the reader to his fuller treatment of the agony in the parallel chapter of Matthew; Wesley names the garden likewise.

Ellicott notes that the description of the customary resort agrees both with Luke’s own earlier statement and with John, and that the long discourses of the fourth Gospel are to be inserted at this point; the stone’s cast he takes for a descriptive touch implying a report from an eyewitness and peculiar to Luke, and the tense of the verb of praying for continuous and sustained prayer. In the words of submission he hears a distinct echo of the prayer Christ had taught his disciples, since he too could say lead us not into temptation, though subject now explicitly, as always implicitly, to the antecedent condition that it be in harmony with the doing of the Father’s will. Robertson explains that Judas undertook the betrayal without waiting for the crowds to disperse precisely because he knew this habit of Jesus, presses the aorist infinitive of the charge as keep on praying not to enter, not even once, holds that this is real temptation and not merely trial so that the words throw light on the petition of the Lord’s Prayer, observes that Luke says nothing of the eight left at the entrance or the three taken further in, and reconciles the falling on the ground of one Gospel with the falling on the face of another as true at different moments.

Theophylact marks that after supper our Lord betakes himself not to idleness or sleep but to prayer and teaching. Chrysostom notes that every art is set forth by the words and the works of him who teaches it, so that our Lord, having come to teach no ordinary virtue, having commanded them in words to pray also does the same in deed; and he denies both the readings that would make the petition a confession of ignorance or a refusal of the Passion, since the knowledge of the Father’s pleasure was no harder than the knowledge of the Father’s substance which he alone clearly knew, and since he had rebuked as Satan a disciple who wished to prevent that Passion.

Cyril of Alexandria sets the rhythm of those days, that by day Christ was in Jerusalem and when the darkness of night came on he held converse with his disciples on the mount of Olives, and observes that you will everywhere find him praying apart, to teach us that we should speak with the most high God with a devout mind and a quiet heart; he did not betake himself to prayer as one wanting another’s help, being himself the almighty power of the Father. Gregory of Nyssa asks what the bending of the knees means, and answers that it is the way of men to pray to their superiors with their faces to the ground, testifying that the greater are those who are asked, whereas human nature contains nothing worthy of God’s imitation, so that the tokens of respect we show one another we have transferred to the humiliation of the incomparable Nature; he who bore our sicknesses bent his knee by reason of the manhood he assumed, giving us an example that we should not exalt ourselves at the time of prayer. Against Apollinaris, who asserted that Christ had no will of his own according to his earthly nature but only the will of God descending from heaven, he asks what will it can then be that God would by no means have fulfilled. Athanasius finds here a double will, one human and of the flesh, which through the weakness of the flesh refuses the Passion, the other divine, which eagerly embraced it since it was not possible that he should be holden of death.

Bede observes that, being about to be betrayed by his own disciple, our Lord goes to the place of his wonted retirement where he might most easily be found, and that he rightly led men about to be instructed in the mysteries of his Body to the mount of Olives, to signify that all who are baptized into his death should be comforted with the anointing of the Holy Spirit. He weighs the form of the charge to pray, since it is impossible for the soul of man not to be tempted, and therefore Christ says not pray that you be not tempted but pray that you enter not into temptation, that is, that the temptation do not at the last overcome you. Over the cup he offers a reading of his own, that Christ begs its removal not from any fear of suffering but from compassion for the first people, lest they should have to drink the cup he had drunk first, and that he says expressly not remove the cup but this cup, the cup of a people who can plead no ignorance in slaying him, having the Law and the Prophets daily prophesying of him.

debates: Why Christ asked that the cup might pass: Bede refers the petition to compassion for the people who would have to drink it rather than to any fear of suffering, Chrysostom denies that it can mean either ignorance of the Father’s pleasure or a refusal of the Passion, and Athanasius makes it the human will refusing through the weakness of the flesh while the divine will embraced it

What the kneeling signifies: Gregory of Nyssa holds that the gesture by which men own an inferior place has been transferred to the incomparable Nature, and that Christ bent the knee by reason of the manhood he assumed as an example against exalting ourselves in prayer, while Robertson treats the varying postures in the Gospels as successive moments of one prayer
outliers: Cyril of Alexandria notes that Christ always prayed apart though, being the almighty power of the Father, he needed no help from another
Ellicott holds that the long discourses of the fourth Gospel belong at this point in the narrative
Gregory of Nyssa uses the petition itself as an argument against Apollinaris, asking what will it could be that God would by no means have fulfilled

43.pericope_label: The angel in the garden, the bloody sweat, and the disciples sleeping for sorrow

schools.summary: Gill declines to guess whether the angel was Michael or Gabriel, holding only that it was certainly a good angel sent from heaven and in a visible form, since Christ is said to have seen him. The agony he makes a conflict and combat with the devil, who now appeared visibly in a horrible form: after the temptations in the wilderness Satan left him for a season until another opportunity should offer, and now the prince of this world attacked him in a garden, where the first onset on human nature had been made, so that the battle between the serpent and the seed of the woman was joined which issued in the destruction of Satan and the recovery of mankind.

Clarke argues that the fullest evidence had to be given of both natures, the miracles attesting the divinity and the hunger, weariness, agony, death and burial the humanity, so that as man Christ needs the assistance of an angel to support a body worn down by fatigue and suffering; the word for agony he takes, with Kypke, to point out the utmost anguish and grief of soul, and he rejects as unlikely the softer reading which makes only the size of the drops the point of the comparison. Wesley says the angel strengthened him lest his body should sink and die before the time, and has him grappling with the powers of darkness, feeling the weight of the wrath of God and at the same time surrounded by a mighty host of devils exercising all their force and malice on his wounded spirit, so that the sweat was forced out of the pores by the vehement distress of his soul.

Ellicott records that these verses are omitted by not a few of the best manuscripts while judging the balance of evidence in their favour, observes that the angel appeared to our Lord only and not to the disciples, who would have seen the new strength in a new expression and look, and notes that the noun for agony describes a conflict rather than mere physical pain and that the four words Luke uses here occur nowhere else in the New Testament and are such as a medical writer would naturally use, the form of the comparison leaving it uncertain whether it applies to manner or to appearance. He finds it characteristic of Luke that where the other Gospels state the fact of the disciples’ sleep he assigns it to its cause, prolonged sorrow having a numbing effect, and that he omits the threefold prayer and the words half permissive and half reproof. Barnes meets the objection that an angel’s comfort would disprove Christ’s divinity, since it was the human nature that suffered and it is the manner of God to sustain the afflicted by such intervention. Robertson notes that angels came after the three temptations whereas here the angel comes during the conflict, glosses the drops as thick clotted blood in a word common in medical works, records the absence of the passage from some ancient documents and the ancient reports of a bloody sweat in Aristotle and Theophrastus, and observes that Luke omits the three turnings to the trusted three and gives the reproach without the bitter details of the other two. Lightfoot refuses outright to say or imagine that God was angry or conceived any indignation against Christ, and would ascribe the bloody sweat to the bite of that old serpent rather than to any apprehension of divine wrath, citing a passage of Diodorus about serpents whose bite brings on an issue of sweat like blood.

Theophylact takes the angel as a lesson in the power of prayer, made known to us that we may exercise it in adversity; on the sweat he offers the softer reading that it is proverbially said of one who has sweated intensely that he sweated blood, the evangelist taking drops of blood as an example of large drops. The charge to pray he glosses as meaning that not to be led into temptation is not to be overwhelmed by it, or else that Christ simply bids us pray that our life may be quiet, since it is presumptuous and of the devil for a man to throw himself into temptation, and James accordingly said not cast yourselves into temptation but, when you are fallen, count it all joy, making a voluntary act out of an involuntary one. Chrysostom observes that because Christ took our flesh in reality and not in appearance he submits, in confirmation of the truth of the dispensation, to bear human things, and that it was midnight and the disciples’ eyes were heavy from grief, their sleep being not of drowsiness but of sorrow.

Bede reads the angel’s visit as a testimony to both natures, since angels are said both to have ministered to Christ and to have comforted him, the Creator needing no protection from his creature, but being made man he is sad for our sakes and for our sakes comforted; he holds too that what follows proves Christ had been praying for his disciples, whom he now exhorts by watching and prayer to be partakers of his prayer. Augustine leaves the cause of the sweat aside and reads the sign, that our Lord praying with a bloody sweat represented the martyrdoms which should flow from his whole body, which is the Church; and he observes, as a harmonist must, that Luke has not stated after which of the prayers Christ came to his disciples.

debates: What caused the agony and the bloody sweat: Wesley makes it the weight of the wrath of God together with a host of devils, Gill a renewed and visible assault of Satan in a garden, Lightfoot expressly refuses to allow that God was angry with Christ at all and ascribes the sweat to the bite of the old serpent, while Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson treat it as a physical effect described in medical vocabulary

Whether these verses belong to the Gospel: Ellicott records that not a few of the best manuscripts omit them and judges the balance of evidence in their favour, and Robertson likewise notes their absence from some ancient documents while treating them as text
outliers: Lightfoot supports the possibility of a bloody sweat from a passage of Diodorus about serpents whose bite brings on an issue of sweat like blood
Augustine turns the sweat into a figure of the martyrdoms that were to flow from the whole body of Christ, which is the Church

47.pericope_label: The betrayer’s kiss: Judas at the head of the multitude, and the arrest begun

schools.summary: Gill marks only the moment, that the multitude and Judas appeared while Christ was still speaking the foregoing words to his disciples.

Henry sets the arrest in a longer war, Satan having been baffled in his attempt to terrify our Lord and put him out of the possession of his own soul, and betaking himself according to his usual method to force and arms, bringing a party into the field to seize him. He follows the sign itself, that the band did not know which was he, so that Judas told them whomsoever he kissed was the man and drew near according to that wonted freedom and familiarity to which our Lord admitted his disciples; and he asks whether anything can be a greater affront or grief to the Lord Jesus than that the badge of friendship should be made the instrument of treachery, and a love-token so desecrated and abused.

Robertson notes that Judas went in front, leading the band because he knew the place well. Lightfoot studies the traitor’s mind: our Saviour had to do with a frightful and terrifying devil, but this man seems possessed with a tame and gentle one, since he converses with the apostles without any token of a devil dwelling in him, and is present at the Passover, at the eucharist and at the very lips of Christ with no sign of Satan being his inmate; but when once the devil has done his work by a man, then let him take heed of his devil. He then frames the gentlest opinion the matter will bear, that Judas may have thought it impossible for Christ to be apprehended, having seen him work such stupendous miracles and more than once deliver himself strangely; that he may have named the sign scoffingly, believing they could never lay hold of him; and that when he saw him condemned he repented, never having suspected that matters would go so far, but presuming that Christ would easily escape and he himself be thirty pieces the richer.

Chrysostom explains why no warning had stopped Judas, since as incurable wounds yield neither to severe nor to soothing remedies, so a soul once taken captive and sold to some particular sin reaps no benefit from admonition; yet he draws the opposite lesson for us, that we must not cease to admonish our brethren though nothing come of our words, since streams flow on though no one drinks of them, and the fisherman who draws empty nets all day takes a fish at evening, and our Lord himself, knowing that Judas would not be converted, ceased not to do what had reference to him. He notes too that Christ gives the traitor his proper name like one lamenting and recalling him rather than one provoked to anger. Theophylact turns to the disciples, inflamed with zeal and unsheathing their swords, and asks whence they had swords at all unless because they had slain the lamb and were come from the feast; the others ask whether they should strike, but Peter, always fervent in his Master’s defence, waits for no permission.

Cyril of Alexandria hears contempt in the phrasing, since the evangelist says he that was called Judas as though holding the name in abhorrence, and yet adds one of the twelve to signify the enormity of the traitor, for one who had been honoured as an apostle became the cause of the murder of Christ; and he adds that, unmindful of the glory of Christ, Judas thought to act secretly, daring to make an especial token of love the instrument of his treachery.

The Gloss marks the turn, that having told of the prayer of Christ Luke goes on to speak of his betrayal, in which he is betrayed by his own disciple. Ambrose takes the following words as a question in which Christ arrests the traitor with a lover’s affection, asking whether he inflicts a wound with the pledge of love, and finds in the title Son of man a whole argument: here is a great manifestation of divine power and a great discipline of virtue, that the traitor’s design is detected and yet forbearance is not withheld, since by manifesting what was hidden he shows whom Judas betrays and by naming the Son of man declares whom he delivers up, the human flesh and not the divine nature being seized; what most confounds the ungrateful is the thought that he had delivered up one who, being the Son of God, for our sakes wished to be the Son of man. He adds that our Lord returned the kiss, not to teach us to dissemble, but that he might not seem to shrink from the traitor and might move him the more by not denying him the offices of love. Augustine orders the three sayings, that the Lord first spoke the words Luke gives, then those Matthew gives, and last those John records. Bede answers with the last word of the scene, that the Lord is never forgetful of his loving kindness, and that while they are bringing death upon the righteous he heals the wounds of his persecutors.

debates: How far Judas is to be excused: Lightfoot frames the gentlest construction the matter will bear, that Judas may have believed Christ could not be taken and named the sign in scorn, while Chrysostom holds that a soul sold to a particular sin is past the reach of admonition, and Cyril of Alexandria charges him with daring to make the token of love the instrument of treason

What the returned kiss means: Ambrose insists that Christ kissed the traitor not to teach dissimulation but to avoid seeming to shrink from him and to move him by not withholding the offices of love, while Chrysostom finds the naming of Judas the accent of lament rather than of anger
outliers: Chrysostom argues that admonition should not cease for want of visible fruit, since streams flow on though nobody drinks and the fisherman who draws empty nets all day takes a fish at evening
Lightfoot observes that the devil in Judas was a tame and gentle one until his work was done, and warns that this is the moment to fear him

48.pericope_label: The question to the traitor, the sword and the ear, and the hour of the power of darkness

schools.summary: Gill hears the name itself as the reproach, since Christ calls him Judas that he might know he was known and to aggravate the sin, addressing him as an apostle, a friend, a familiar friend in whom he had trusted; he takes the names of Peter and Malchus from John, and has Christ turning to the chief priests, members of the sanhedrim, only after the miracle had quieted the mob and kept them from cutting the apostles to pieces. Calvin gives the healing a motive of another kind: by his foolish zeal Peter had brought grievous reproach on his Master and his doctrine, and there is no doubt this was a contrivance by which Satan attempted to involve the Gospel in eternal disgrace, as though Christ had kept company with assassins and seditious men for revolutionary purposes, so that Christ healed the wound Peter had inflicted; and a fearful and amazing stupidity must have seized the adversaries, who were not at all affected by having seen such a miracle.

Clarke asks whether Judas attempts to kiss him as a friend while delivering him into the hands of his enemies, and says we need not wonder since Satan had entered into his heart. On the disputed words he suggests they may mean suffer me to go thus far, the crowd having a firm hold of Christ while he sought leave to reach Malchus and heal him, though they may equally be addressed to the disciples, telling them to make no resistance since only so are the Scriptures to be fulfilled. The hour he makes the whole point: it is the time in which the priests are permitted to unrein their malice, which they could not do before because God did not permit it, and so perfectly are they under his control that neither they nor the prince of darkness can proceed a hair’s breadth except by that permission, which he calls a comfortable thought for the followers of Christ. Wesley reads the question to Judas as turning on knowledge, he whom thou knowest to be the Son of man, observes that the chief priests and captains and elders all came of their own accord while the soldiers and servants were sent, and glosses the hour as the time before which they could not take him and the time when Satan has power.

Barnes makes every word of the question emphatic in turn, dost thou violate all thy obligations of fidelity, thou who hast been so long with him and so much favoured, and dost thou betray the Son of man, the Messiah, the hope of the nations. Ellicott notes that all three of the first Gospels record the kiss but Luke alone the question, and traces a twofold purpose in the title, since it was the old familiar name that appealed to memory and conscience and also the name connected with the office of Judge and King, so that it came as a warning of the retribution the traitor was preparing for himself; the phrase for those who spoke he finds chosen as more accurate than the disciples would have been, he leaves the disputed command open between the disciples and the officers while inclining to the latter because the immediate healing tends to conciliation, he prefers the rendering robber with swords and clubs, and he holds that in identifying the power working through human instruments with darkness our Lord virtually claims to be himself the Light. Robertson observes that Jesus challenges the act openly and calls it betrayal without stopping it, that Luke alone gives the disciples’ question and alone as a physician says the right ear, John following him in that and adding the names of Peter and Malchus probably because both were dead by then and Peter could no longer be brought into trouble; he prefers to refer the disputed command to the disciples, notes that we are not told whether Christ picked up the severed piece since he could have healed without it, and that this miracle of surgery is given by Luke alone, and finds the surrender voluntary, the moral value of the atoning sacrifice lying in that voluntariness. Lightfoot presses the other side of the same hour, that the serpent himself is now come in Judas and the seed of the serpent is the rout that came with him, to whom it was fatal to bruise the heel of the Messiah, that the thing and its instruments were alike foretold and predetermined, and that now all fences lie open and the chains of the devil himself are loosed, so that he may exert all his furies at pleasure without the least check or restraint of divine providence.

Cyril of Jerusalem, gathering the testimonies of the Passion for hearers met not to hear a speculative exposition of the Scriptures but to be certified of what they already believe, begins where the Passion began: Judas was the traitor, and he came against him and stood, speaking words of peace but plotting war.

debates: To whom the words suffer ye thus far are addressed: Clarke suggests they mean suffer me to go thus far, a request to be allowed to reach the wounded man, Ellicott leaves the question open between the disciples and the officers while inclining to the officers because the healing tends to conciliation, and Robertson refers them to the disciples as being told to bear this much violence against their Master

How far the licence of this hour extends: Clarke and Wesley make it a permission strictly bounded, so that neither men nor the prince of darkness can move a hair’s breadth further than God allows, while Lightfoot has every fence thrown open and the devil’s own chains loosed for the occasion, and Robertson reads the whole surrender as voluntary
outliers: Robertson explains that John alone names Peter and Malchus because by the time he wrote both were dead and the naming could no longer bring Peter into danger
Calvin makes the healing of the ear a defence of the Gospel’s reputation, lest Christ should be thought to have kept company with assassins for revolutionary ends

54.pericope_label: Peter follows afar off: the fire in the court, the three denials, and the look that broke him

schools.summary: Gill notes that they laid hold of Christ notwithstanding the miracle and the humanity he had just shown in healing the servant’s ear, and that this was itself a confirmation of his last words, since now was their hour and power was given them as the emissaries of Satan. He explains the fire, since it was cold in the night even at the passover and the beginning of harvest, and the servants kindled it in the middle of the hall while Jesus was examined at the other end; and he has Peter, startled at the maid’s positive assertion and seeing no other way to clear himself, deny roundly at once, so that the man who had said he would die with his Master is frighted by a servant maid, and falls at last to cursing and swearing.

Henry traces the stages of the fall. It began in sneaking, for Peter followed his Master when he was led away prisoner, which showed a concern for him, but followed afar off that he might be out of danger, thinking to trim the matter, to follow Christ and so satisfy his conscience but to follow afar off and so save his reputation and sleep in a whole skin; it proceeded in keeping his distance still and associating himself with the high priest’s servants. He notes too that even when the enemies had seized their prey they were in confusion, taking him the furthest way about, or rather not knowing which way they hurried him.

Clarke observes that the maid beheld Peter attentively by the help of the light of the fire at which he sat, notes the delicacy of the reproof conveyed in the look, and reports that the name of Peter is omitted in the last verse by many good manuscripts and is left out of the text by Griesbach. Wesley harmonises the accounts by distributing the charge among several accusers, the maid who led him in first putting the question and then affirming it positively, another maid accusing him to the bystanders and so giving occasion to the man here mentioned to renew the charge; and he remarks that in the whole hour that intervened Peter did not recollect himself.
