Ellicott prefers court-yard to hall, our word suggesting a covered space inside the house, notes that the phrase is literally by the light or blaze and that the maid’s steady gaze is expressed by Luke’s characteristic word, and adds that it is from John’s narrative that we learn why she said this man also, John having already been seen and known as a disciple. He observes that the vocative rendered Man always implies a touch of anger or impatience, that both the phrase for an hour having intervened and the word for confidently affirmed are peculiar to Luke, and that the glance which was the turning point of Peter’s life is mentioned by Luke alone, our Lord looking on the disciple as he was being led from Annas to the more public trial before the Sanhedrin. Robertson observes that Luke alone mentions the house, glosses the verb of kindling as making a fire that blazes all round and remarks that it was April and cool at night, doubts that the denials in the four accounts can be co-ordinated at all unless several joined in when one led off, notes that each denial tangles Peter further, calls the picture of the look graphic and Luke’s alone, and reports that a few old Latin documents omit the last verse though the evidence for rejection is too slight, the aorist being ingressive, so that Peter burst into tears.

Chrysostom finds the great zeal of Peter in his not flying when he saw all the others do so, and adds that he rightly followed afar off, being soon to deny, for he could never have denied had he clung close to Christ, yet that he must be revered for not forsaking his Lord even when he was afraid, since fear is the effect of nature and solicitude of tender affection. He bids us marvel at the Master, who though himself a prisoner exercised such forethought for his disciple that by a single look he brought him to himself and provoked him to tears.

Cyril of Alexandria, looking back over the whole betrayal, finds that many and bitter passions wage war with the soul of man and attack it with unendurable violence, but that worse than all the rest is that root of all evil, the love of money, into whose inextricable nets the traitorous disciple so fell that he consented to become the minister of the devil’s guile and the instrument of the wicked chiefs of the synagogue.

Ambrose guards the first clause, that when we read of Jesus being holden we should not think him holden in respect of his divine nature, or unwilling through weakness, since he is held captive and bound according to the truth of his bodily nature. Bede identifies the chief priest as Caiaphas, makes Peter’s following afar off a figure of the Church, which follows and imitates the Passion but at a great distance, and reads the hour itself, since Peter who sinned at midnight repented at cock-crow, correcting by the remembrance of the true light the error he had committed in the darkness of forgetfulness; he adds that Christ is denied not only by the man who says he is not the Christ but by the Christian who says he is not one. Augustine notes that Christ was first led to Annas and then to Caiaphas though Mark and Luke give no name, warns that the look requires careful consideration since Peter was outside in the court among those warming themselves while the trial went on within, so that the looking upon him seems to have been done in a divine manner, and takes the cock mystically for some great teacher who rouses the listless and sleepy.

debates: How the look was given: Augustine argues that it cannot have been with the bodily face, since Peter was outside in the court while the trial went on in the inner part of the house, and concludes that it was done in a divine manner, whereas Ellicott places it physically, our Lord being led across from Annas to the Sanhedrin at that moment

How the denials are to be harmonised: Wesley distributes them among several accusers in a fixed order, while Robertson doubts that the four accounts can be co-ordinated at all unless others joined in when one led off, and notes that the accuser here is a man where the other Gospels have a maid
outliers: Bede holds that Christ is denied not only by the man who says he is not the Christ but by the Christian who says that he himself is not one
Augustine reads the cock mystically as a great teacher who rouses the listless and the sleepy
Clarke and Robertson both record manuscript evidence against the last verse, the name of Peter being absent from many good copies and the whole verse from a few old Latin documents

63.pericope_label: The mocking of the prophet, the second hearing before the Sanhedrin, and the confession

schools.summary: Gill has the men who held Jesus either Roman soldiers or the servants of the high priest, keeping their grip on him lest he should get away, though there was no reason for it, since his time was come and he would not escape though he could easily have rescued himself; he lists the blasphemies spoken against him, the denial and ridicule of his deity and divine sonship, the burlesquing of his offices of prophet, priest and king, and the charges of being a profane sinner, a sabbath breaker and one that had a devil. At the end he has the whole sanhedrim speaking with one voice, greedy to lay hold of the words and to have something to lay to his charge.

Henry presses the cruelty of the scene, that the rude and barbarous servants who held Jesus in custody till the court sat would not allow him to repose himself one minute though he had had no sleep all night, nor to compose himself though he was hurried to his trial with no time to prepare for it; they made sport with him, so that this sorrowful night to him was a merry night to them, and the blessed Jesus, like Samson, was made the fool in the play, hoodwinked and struck on the face in a children’s game, with the affront aimed at his prophetic office.

Clarke marks the difference of order, these verses being placed by Matthew and Mark before the account of Peter’s denial, puts the refusal bluntly, that even if they could give no answer proving him not to be the Christ they would not let him go, since he knew they were determined to put him to death, takes the word rendered hereafter to mean that from this very time the kingdom of God is going to be set up, and observes at the close that they had now gone as far as they could, since the Jews had no power to put him to death and he must be brought before Pilate. Wesley suggests that Christ was probably abused in the same manner both before and after his condemnation, since the other evangelists place this after the condemnation, and turns the charge of blasphemy round upon the accusers, since they charged him with it because he said he was the Son of God while the evangelist fixes the charge on them, because he really was so.

Robertson notes that the verb for holding is used here alone in the New Testament of keeping a prisoner, that the imperfect of mocking is inchoative, they began to mock and to play like boys, that this is the second appearance before the Sanhedrin, merely mentioned by Mark and Matthew who give the first in detail, and that the word for the assembly is the technical term for the eldership. He holds that Jesus answers their demand about the Messiah by asserting that he is the Son of man, that they so understand him, and that the three titles are used as practical equivalents, so that he accepts the challenge and admits the claim to all three; and he closes with the alternative, that they were right if Jesus is not what he claimed to be and eternally wrong because he is. Ellicott traces the taunt of the blindfolded prophet to the popular view of a lower Judaism which identified prophecy with clairvoyance, records what Luke passes over of the trial, the false witnesses who did not agree and the charge about the Temple and the silence until the adjuration, notes that the answer about their unbelief is reported by Luke alone and is interpreted by John, finds in Christ’s own unanswered question about David’s son the reference of the next clause, so that the words are an indirect protest against their claim to question him, renders the promise as from this time forth shall the Son of man be sitting, and admits that in Luke’s shorter record the confession follows the apparent refusal with hardly any consistency, Matthew showing that the change was caused by the adjuration of the high priest.

Chrysostom sets the scene under one word, that the Lord of heaven and earth sustains and suffers the mockings of the ungodly, giving us an example of patience. Theophylact adds that the Lord of prophets is derided as a false prophet, and that they blindfolded him not so that he should not see their wickedness but that they might hide his face from them, while he who was struck with the blows of the Jews is struck now by the blasphemies of false Christians; he says too that Christ knew the secrets of their hearts, that those who had not believed his works would much less believe his words, hears the answer as a closing of all discourse, since no time is left for teaching but hereafter comes the time of judgment, and draws the moral that the disobedient reap no advantage when the more secret mysteries are revealed to them but rather incur the heavier punishment, so that such things ought to be concealed from them.
Cyril of Alexandria notes that when Christ spoke this the company of the Pharisees were very wroth and uttered shameful words.

Augustine notes that the mockings of our Lord and the temptation of Peter are not related by all the evangelists in the same order, since Matthew and Mark mention the mockings first and then Peter’s temptation while Luke describes the temptation first. Bede recalls that Christ had often declared himself the Christ, as when he said that he and the Father are one, and had asked them how they called the Christ the son of David when David in the Spirit called him Lord, though they wished neither to believe his words nor to answer his questions; and he notes that they understood him to be calling himself the Son of God in the words about sitting at the right hand of the power of God. Ambrose observes that the Lord had rather prove himself a King than call himself one, that they might have no excuse for condemning him when they confess the truth of that which they lay against him.

debates: Where the mocking belongs in the order of events: Augustine records that Matthew and Mark put it before the denial and Luke after, Clarke marks the same displacement, and Wesley suggests that Christ was probably abused in the same manner both before and after the condemnation

Why Christ answers at last after seeming to refuse: Ellicott admits that Luke’s sequence is hardly consistent and supplies from Matthew the adjuration of the high priest which left no alternative of silence, Theophylact makes the refusal a declaration that the time for discourse is over and the time of judgment at hand, and Clarke makes it a recognition that they were determined on his death whatever he said
outliers: Henry compares the blindfolded Christ to Samson made the fool in the play, the servants turning his sorrowful night into their own merriment
Theophylact concludes that the more secret mysteries ought to be concealed from the disobedient, since revealing them brings not advantage but a heavier punishment
Wesley turns the charge of blasphemy back on the accusers, since the evangelist calls their words blasphemy for the very reason that Christ was in truth the Son of God
